practice_questions.text:
A student views an onion cell under a light microscope. The image of the cell measures 24 mm. The actual size of the cell is 0.04 mm.
Calculate the magnification used. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Magnification = image size ÷ real size [1 mark]
Magnification = 24 ÷ 0.04 = ×600 [1 mark]
(Accept correct working with answer in any equivalent form; mark cannot be awarded without a numerical answer.)

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the structure of a sperm cell is adapted to its function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear adaptations each with a full causal explanation, e.g. 'The midpiece is packed with mitochondria, which carry out aerobic respiration to transfer energy for the movement of the flagellum' and 'The acrosome contains enzymes that digest the egg cell membrane, allowing the sperm nucleus to enter and fertilise the egg.' (4 marks)
Secure: Two adaptations with partial explanation, e.g. 'Many mitochondria to provide energy for swimming; long flagellum for movement.' (3 marks)
Developing: One well-explained adaptation or two stated without explanation. (2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Describe how you would use a light microscope to prepare and view a sample of cheek cells. Include how to obtain a clear, well-focused image.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Chronological method covering: smear cells on slide, add methylene blue stain to make nuclei visible, lower coverslip at an angle (to prevent air bubbles distorting image), clip slide on stage, begin on lowest power objective, use coarse focus then fine focus to sharpen image, switch to higher power using fine focus only. Control variable stated (e.g. same stain concentration). (6 marks)
Secure: Covers most key steps including stain use, coverslip technique and focusing sequence. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Several steps present but gaps in method (e.g. no mention of stain or air bubble prevention). (2–3 marks)
Emerging: Basic procedure described without key details. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: A bacterium has a diameter of 3 μm. Express this measurement in metres, giving your answer in standard form.
practice_questions.marks:
Conversion: 3 μm = 3 × 10⁻⁶ m [1 mark for correct conversion, 1 mark for correct standard form]
(Accept 3 × 10⁻⁶ m. Do not accept 0.000003 m alone without standard form.)

before.content_html:
Enzymes and the Active Site

Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts — they speed up chemical reactions inside living organisms without being used up. Each enzyme has a specific three-dimensional shape with an indentation called the active site. The active site’s shape is precisely complementary to one particular substrate molecule.

The lock and key model describes how the substrate (key) fits into the active site (lock) of the enzyme. Once bound, the enzyme catalyses the reaction, and the products are released. The enzyme is then free to catalyse another reaction. Because each enzyme’s active site has a unique shape, enzymes are said to be substrate-specific.

Key Fact

Enzymes are proteins with a specific active site that is complementary to one substrate. The lock and key model explains substrate specificity. At the optimum temperature and pH, the reaction rate is highest. Outside this range, enzyme activity decreases.

Temperature and pH Effects

Temperature affects enzyme activity in two ways. As temperature rises towards the optimum, molecules have more kinetic energy, collide more frequently and form enzyme–substrate complexes faster — so the rate of reaction increases. Above the optimum, the enzyme’s structure is disrupted: bonds maintaining the active site break, and the shape changes permanently. This is called denaturation. Unlike inhibition, denaturation is irreversible.

pH also affects enzyme activity. Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which the active site shape is maintained. Extreme pH (too acidic or too alkaline) denatures the enzyme by altering the bonds that hold its three-dimensional shape. For example, pepsin (a stomach enzyme) works best at pH 2, while amylase in the mouth works best at pH 7.

In a typical enzyme investigation, amylase is mixed with starch solution at a range of pH values (using buffer solutions to maintain each pH). Iodine solution is used to test for starch: it turns blue-black in the presence of starch and remains orange-brown when starch has been fully broken down.

You measure how long it takes for the iodine to stop turning blue-black (i.e. the starch has all been digested). A shorter time means a faster rate of reaction. The independent variable is pH; the dependent variable is the time taken for the colour change. Control variables include temperature (maintained by a water bath), concentration of enzyme and starch, and volume of solutions. Note: a thermometer measures temperature — it does not control it. The water bath controls temperature.

To calculate the rate of reaction: $$\text{rate} = \frac{1}{\text{time (s)}} \times 1000 \quad (\text{in arbitrary units})$$

Diffusion and Osmosis

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration — down the concentration gradient. It is passive: no energy is required. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across gas exchange surfaces in the lungs; glucose diffuses from the gut into blood cells.

Factors affecting diffusion rate: concentration gradient (steeper gradient, faster diffusion), temperature (higher temperature, more kinetic energy, faster diffusion), surface area (larger area, more diffusion) and distance (shorter distance, faster diffusion).

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential. It is a type of diffusion, but refers specifically to water. Plant cells placed in distilled water gain mass (water enters by osmosis); in concentrated sugar solution they lose mass.

Key Fact

Diffusion: net movement of particles down a concentration gradient — no energy needed. Osmosis: movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from high to low water potential — no energy needed. Active transport: movement of particles against the concentration gradient — energy from respiration required.

Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient — from low to high concentration. This requires energy from cellular respiration (ATP produced in mitochondria). Examples: root hair cells absorb mineral ions from the soil even though the soil concentration is lower than inside the root; glucose is absorbed from the small intestine into the blood even when the gut glucose concentration is already lower than in the blood.

Potato cylinders (equal length and mass) are placed in solutions of different sucrose concentrations. After a set time, each cylinder is dried and reweighed. The change in mass (or percentage change) is calculated:

$$\text{percentage change in mass} = \frac{\text{final mass} - \text{initial mass}}{\text{initial mass}} \times 100$$

Cylinders in distilled water gain mass (water enters by osmosis). Cylinders in concentrated sucrose solution lose mass (water leaves by osmosis). The concentration at which there is no change in mass is the water potential of the potato cells. Percentage change is used rather than absolute change so that results from cylinders of slightly different starting masses can be compared fairly.

Food Tests (Triple Only)

You are required to know four chemical food tests. Each identifies a specific food molecule using a reagent and a colour change.

Iodine test for starch: Add iodine solution to the food sample. Blue-black colour = starch present; orange-brown = no starch.

Benedict’s test for reducing sugars (e.g. glucose): Add Benedict’s solution and heat in a water bath. Brick-red (or orange/yellow) precipitate = reducing sugar present; remains blue = no reducing sugar.

Biuret test for protein: Add biuret reagent (sodium hydroxide then copper sulfate solution) to the food sample. Purple/violet colour = protein present; remains blue = no protein.

Emulsion (ethanol) test for lipid: Dissolve food in ethanol, then add water. A white, cloudy emulsion = lipid present; remains clear = no lipid.

Calorimetry is used to measure the energy content of foods. A food sample is burned and the heat energy released is used to raise the temperature of a known volume of water. The energy content is calculated using: $$Q = mc\Delta T$$ where \(m\) is the mass of water in grams, \(c\) is the specific heat capacity of water (4.2 J g1 °C1), and \(\Delta T\) is the temperature rise in °C.

Key Fact

Iodine → blue-black for starch. Benedict’s (heated) → brick-red for reducing sugars. Biuret → purple for protein. Ethanol emulsion → white cloudy for lipid.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by denaturation of an enzyme?
practice_questions.marks: A permanent change in the shape of the enzyme's active site [1 mark] so that the substrate can no longer bind / the enzyme can no longer function. (Do not accept 'the enzyme is destroyed' without reference to shape change.)

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates the effect of sucrose concentration on the mass of potato cylinders. The table shows her results:

Sucrose concentration (mol/dm³) | Initial mass (g) | Final mass (g)
0.0 | 2.8 | 3.2
0.2 | 2.9 | 3.0
0.6 | 3.1 | 2.8

Calculate the percentage change in mass for the 0.6 mol/dm³ solution. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Percentage change = (2.8 − 3.1) ÷ 3.1 × 100 [1 mark for correct substitution]
= −9.7% (accept −9.68% to −9.7%) [1 mark for correct answer with negative sign indicating mass loss]

practice_questions.text:
A food sample is tested with Benedict's solution and heated in a water bath. The solution turns brick-red.
Identify which food molecule is present and explain what this colour change indicates.
practice_questions.marks:
Food molecule: reducing sugar (e.g. glucose) [1 mark]
Explanation: Benedict's reagent is reduced by the sugar, forming a brick-red copper(I) oxide precipitate [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain why active transport requires energy but diffusion does not.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Diffusion moves particles down the concentration gradient (from high to low), which is energetically favourable and occurs spontaneously. Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient (from low to high), which is not spontaneous and requires energy from cellular respiration (ATP from mitochondria) to power carrier proteins. (4 marks)
Secure: Correct direction for both processes and energy source named (respiration/ATP). (3 marks)
Developing: Correct directions stated but energy source vague ('uses energy from cells'). (2 marks)
Emerging: One correct point, e.g. 'active transport moves against the gradient'. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the effect of temperature on amylase activity. Describe how she should carry out a fair investigation, including how to measure the rate of reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sets up water baths at a range of temperatures; adds buffer solution to starch-amylase mixture to control pH; uses iodine to test for starch at regular intervals; times how long until iodine no longer turns blue-black; calculates rate as 1/time; identifies independent variable (temperature), dependent variable (time for colour change), and controls (pH, starch and enzyme concentration, volume of solutions); repeats for reliability. (6 marks)
Secure: Correct method with most steps, states control variables and rate calculation. (4–5 marks)
Developing: Describes use of water bath and iodine test, but misses controls or rate calculation. (2–3 marks)
Emerging: Refers to temperature and iodine but little method detail. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
'Understanding enzyme denaturation is more useful to biology than understanding diffusion.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Weighs evidence on both sides. For denaturation: explains importance for understanding digestion, body temperature regulation, medical applications (e.g. fever, enzyme inhibitors as drugs). For diffusion: explains role in gas exchange, nutrient absorption, all passive transport in cells. Draws a justified conclusion with criteria stated (e.g. 'diffusion is more fundamental because every cell relies on it constantly, whereas denaturation is a pathological change'). Uses correct terminology throughout. (9 marks)
Secure: Both sides argued with specific biological examples; conclusion present but criteria less explicit. (6–8 marks)
Developing: Both processes described rather than evaluated; little comparison or conclusion. (3–5 marks)
Emerging: One process described with minimal evaluation. (1–2 marks)

lessons.title: Cells and Control: Mitosis, Stem Cells and the Brain

before.content_html:
The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

Cells divide to allow organisms to grow, to repair damaged tissue and to replace worn-out cells. This follows the cell cycle. Most of the cycle is spent in interphase, when the cell grows, manufactures more organelles and replicates all of its DNA so that each daughter cell will receive a complete set of chromosomes.

After interphase, the cell enters mitosis. During mitosis the chromosomes condense and become visible, then the copies are pulled to opposite ends of the cell. The cytoplasm and cell membrane then divide to produce two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the full chromosome complement.

Mitosis has four main phases:

  • Prophase — chromosomes condense and become visible; the nuclear envelope breaks down.
  • Metaphase — chromosomes line up along the centre (equator) of the cell, attached to spindle fibres.
  • Anaphase — spindle fibres contract and pull the chromosome copies to opposite poles.
  • Telophase and cytokinesis — nuclear envelopes reform around each set of chromosomes; the cytoplasm divides, producing two cells.
Key Fact

Mitosis: Prophase (chromosomes condense, nuclear envelope breaks down) → Metaphase (chromosomes align at equator) → Anaphase (copies pulled to poles) → Telophase & cytokinesis (two identical daughter cells form).

Cancer results when the cell cycle is no longer controlled. Cells divide repeatedly and uncontrollably, forming a tumour. Tumours that spread to other parts of the body are called malignant.

Cell Differentiation and Growth

As cells divide and grow, they become specialised through a process called differentiation. Most animal cells differentiate during embryonic development and then lose the ability to become other cell types. Plant cells retain the ability to differentiate throughout life because they have meristem tissue at root and shoot tips.

Growth in organisms can be measured by mass, length or percentage change. In children, growth is monitored using percentile charts. A percentile line, such as the 50th percentile, means that 50% of children of that age have a measurement below that value. Percentile charts allow doctors to identify children whose growth is unusually slow or unusually fast, prompting further investigation.

Stem Cells

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide to produce more stem cells or differentiate into a range of specialised cells. Embryonic stem cells (from the inner cell mass of an early embryo) can differentiate into almost any cell type. Adult stem cells are more limited; bone marrow stem cells, for example, produce all types of blood cell.

Stem cells have potential therapeutic uses: replacing damaged nerve cells in spinal cord injuries, producing insulin-secreting cells to treat diabetes, and growing replacement tissue for burns patients. These therapies are at various stages of research and clinical trials.

Embryonic stem cells raise ethical concerns because extracting them destroys the embryo. Some people argue the embryo is a potential human life and should not be used for research. Others argue that the potential to relieve suffering outweighs this concern. Adult stem cells and stem cells from umbilical cord blood avoid this ethical issue. Plant meristem cells can also be used in tissue culture to grow new plants from a single cell.

Key Fact

Embryonic stem cells can differentiate into any cell type (pluripotent) but their use is controversial because extracting them destroys the embryo. Adult stem cells are less versatile but raise fewer ethical concerns. Plant meristems can generate whole new plants in tissue culture.

The Brain (Triple Only)

The brain controls most of the body’s functions and is made of billions of interconnected neurones. Three key regions you must know are:

  • Cerebral hemispheres (cerebrum) — the largest region. Controls conscious thought, memory, language, personality and voluntary movement. The outer layer (cerebral cortex) is deeply folded to increase surface area.
  • Cerebellum — at the back of the brain. Coordinates balance, posture and precise muscle movements such as riding a bicycle or playing a musical instrument.
  • Medulla oblongata (medulla) — connects the brain to the spinal cord. Controls automatic, life-sustaining functions: breathing rate, heart rate and blood pressure.

Brain research relies on scanning techniques that allow scientists to investigate brain structure and function without surgery.

CT scanning (computed tomography) uses X-rays taken from multiple angles. A computer reconstructs these to produce detailed cross-sectional images of brain structure. CT scans are good for identifying physical abnormalities such as tumours, bleeds or structural damage.

PET scanning (positron emission tomography) uses a radioactive tracer (usually a form of glucose) injected into the blood. Active brain regions use more glucose, so they emit more radiation. The PET scanner detects this and produces a colour-coded map showing which areas of the brain are most active during a particular task. PET scans reveal function rather than structure, making them useful for studying conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease or mapping speech and memory regions before surgery.

practice_questions.text: A child's height measurement falls on the 25th percentile. Explain what this tells a doctor about the child's growth.
practice_questions.marks: 25% of children of the same age are shorter than this child (or 75% are taller) [1 mark]. The child's height is within the normal range and does not immediately indicate a growth problem [1 mark]. (Accept equivalent correct interpretation.)

practice_questions.text: Explain why embryonic stem cells are considered more useful than adult stem cells for medical treatments, and describe one ethical objection to their use.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent — they can differentiate into any cell type in the body, making them potentially useful for replacing any damaged or missing tissue (e.g. nerve cells after spinal injury, insulin-producing cells for diabetes). Adult stem cells are more limited in the types of cell they can become (e.g. bone marrow stem cells only produce blood cells). Ethical objection: extracting embryonic stem cells destroys the embryo, which some people consider to be taking a human life. (4 marks)
Secure: Pluripotency explained, adult stem cell limitation stated, ethical objection identified. (3 marks)

practice_questions.text: Describe the differences between CT scanning and PET scanning in investigating the brain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: CT uses X-rays from multiple angles to create structural images — useful for identifying tumours or bleeds. PET uses a radioactive glucose tracer to produce functional maps showing which brain regions are most active during a task — useful for studying disease or mapping functions. CT shows structure; PET shows function. (4 marks)
Secure: Both techniques described accurately with the structure vs function distinction made. (3 marks)
Developing: One technique accurately described. (2 marks)
Emerging: One simple point, e.g. 'PET uses radioactivity'. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
A student claims: 'Studying the brain is impossible without surgery.'
Using your knowledge of brain scanning, evaluate this claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues clearly against the claim using CT and PET scanning as evidence. Explains what each reveals (structure vs function). Acknowledges that scanning has limitations compared to direct study (e.g. spatial resolution, radiation dose, cost). Notes that some knowledge of brain function came historically from studying people with brain injuries (case study approach). Conclusion is explicit and weighs evidence: scanning has transformed our understanding without surgery but does have limitations. (9 marks)
Secure: Both scanning techniques discussed, limitations acknowledged, justified conclusion. (6–8 marks)
Developing: Both techniques described rather than evaluated; limited conclusion. (3–5 marks)
Emerging: One scanning technique mentioned. (1–2 marks)

lessons.title: Nervous System, Reflexes and the Eye

before.content_html:
Neurones and the Nervous System

The nervous system allows rapid communication across the body using electrical impulses. It has two main divisions: the central nervous system (CNS), consisting of the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system, consisting of the nerves that connect the CNS to the body’s receptors and effectors.

There are three types of neurone:

  • Sensory neurone — carries impulses from receptors (e.g. in the skin, eyes, ears) towards the CNS. Has a long axon and a cell body located outside the spinal cord.
  • Relay neurone — found entirely within the CNS. Connects sensory neurones to motor neurones and processes information within the spinal cord and brain.
  • Motor neurone — carries impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands), causing a response.

Each neurone has a long axon surrounded by a myelin sheath in many neurones. The myelin sheath acts as an electrical insulator and dramatically increases the speed of impulse transmission. Damage to the myelin sheath (as in multiple sclerosis) slows impulse conduction.

Key Fact

Reflex arc sequence: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector (muscle or gland). The myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds up impulse transmission.

Synapses

Neurones do not physically touch each other. The tiny gap between two neurones is called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of a neurone, it triggers the release of chemical messengers called neurotransmitters from small vesicles. These diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to complementary receptor proteins on the next neurone’s membrane. If enough neurotransmitter binds, a new electrical impulse is generated in the next neurone.

Synapses only allow impulses to travel in one direction (because neurotransmitters are released from one side only). Many drugs and toxins work by interfering with neurotransmitter release or reception at synapses.

A reflex is a fast, automatic response to a stimulus that does not require conscious thought. Reflexes bypass the brain, passing through the spinal cord instead, which is why they are so rapid.

Reflex arc pathway: stimulus (e.g. touching a hot surface) → receptor (pain receptors in the skin) → sensory neurone (impulse to spinal cord) → relay neurone (in the spinal cord) → motor neurone (impulse to effector) → effector (muscle contracts, hand withdrawn). The brain receives information about the reflex only after the response has already begun.

The Eye (Triple Only)

The eye is a sense organ that detects light. You must know the function of each structure and how the eye focuses light on the retina.

Cornea — the transparent curved cover at the front. It refracts (bends) most of the incoming light.

Iris — the coloured ring surrounding the pupil. Circular muscles (contract to constrict the pupil in bright light) and radial muscles (contract to dilate the pupil in dim light) control the amount of light entering.

Lens — a transparent flexible disc that fine-tunes the focus of light. It changes shape by the action of the ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments.

Retina — the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. It contains rod cells (sensitive to dim light; detect black and white) and cone cells (sensitive to bright light; detect colour in three wavelengths: red, green, blue). Impulses travel along the optic nerve to the brain.

Accommodation

Accommodation is the eye’s ability to change focus between near and distant objects by altering the shape of the lens. When viewing a near object: the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens becomes rounder (more curved), increasing its refracting power. When viewing a distant object: the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments pull taut and the lens flattens (less curved), reducing its refracting power.

Vision Defects and Correction

Short-sightedness (myopia) occurs when the eyeball is too long or the cornea is too curved. Light from distant objects is focused in front of the retina instead of on it. It is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens that spreads the light rays before they enter the eye.

Long-sightedness (hyperopia) occurs when the eyeball is too short or the cornea is too flat. Light from close objects is focused behind the retina. It is corrected with a convex (converging) lens that brings the light rays together before they enter the eye.

Cataracts form when the lens becomes cloudy, scattering light and reducing vision. The cloudy lens is surgically replaced with an artificial implant. Colour blindness results from a deficiency in one or more types of cone cell. It is sex-linked (carried on the X chromosome) and is much more common in males than females.

Key Fact

Short-sightedness: distant objects blurred; light focused in front of retina; corrected by concave lens. Long-sightedness: near objects blurred; light focused behind retina; corrected by convex lens.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the role of the relay neurone?
A) Carries impulses from receptors to the spinal cord
B) Connects sensory and motor neurones within the CNS
C) Carries impulses from the spinal cord to muscles
D) Releases neurotransmitters into the blood
practice_questions.marks: B) Connects sensory and motor neurones within the CNS [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the function of the myelin sheath.
practice_questions.marks: It insulates the axon and speeds up the transmission of nerve impulses. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a neurotransmitter transmits a signal across a synapse.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Electrical impulse arrives at the end of the pre-synaptic neurone; neurotransmitter is released from vesicles into the synaptic cleft; it diffuses across the gap; binds to complementary receptor proteins on the post-synaptic neurone membrane; triggers a new electrical impulse in the next neurone. Correctly notes one-directional transmission. (4 marks)
Secure: Three or four correct steps, sequence clear. (3 marks)
Developing: Two correct steps, e.g. neurotransmitter released and diffuses. (2 marks)
Emerging: Simple statement that a chemical carries the signal. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text:
A student touches a sharp pin with her finger and immediately pulls her hand away before feeling pain.
Explain how the reflex arc produces this rapid response.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Pain receptors in the skin detect the stimulus; a sensory neurone carries an impulse to the spinal cord; a relay neurone in the spinal cord connects to a motor neurone; the motor neurone carries an impulse to the arm muscles (effector), which contract and withdraw the hand. The response bypasses the brain, so it occurs before the student consciously feels pain. (4 marks)
Secure: Correct pathway named with effector response and bypass of brain explained. (3 marks)
Developing: Correct pathway without full explanation of speed advantage. (2 marks)
Emerging: Mentions sensory and motor neurone but sequence incomplete. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: A patient is diagnosed with short-sightedness. Explain what causes this condition and how it is corrected.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Short-sightedness occurs when the eyeball is too long (or the cornea too curved), causing light from distant objects to be focused in front of the retina rather than on it, producing a blurred image. A concave (diverging) lens is placed in front of the eye; it spreads the light rays so that they are focused further back, on the retina. (4 marks)
Secure: Cause and correction correctly identified with mechanism for the lens type. (3 marks)
Developing: Cause stated (eyeball too long) and type of lens named without explanation of mechanism. (2 marks)
Emerging: Identifies that a concave lens is used. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and limitations of using spectacles compared with laser eye surgery to correct short-sightedness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Spectacles — non-invasive, reversible, cheap, require no recovery time; limitations include inconvenience, risk of breaking or losing, may be uncomfortable. Laser eye surgery — permanent correction by reshaping the cornea; no need for glasses; limitations include cost, surgical risk (infection, complications), not reversible, not suitable for all patients (e.g. thin corneas). A justified conclusion weighing safety vs convenience vs permanence. (9 marks)
Secure: Both options evaluated with specific points on each side and conclusion. (6–8 marks)
Developing: Both options described rather than evaluated; limited conclusion. (3–5 marks)
Emerging: One option described. (1–2 marks)

lessons.title: Genetics: DNA, Inheritance and Punnett Squares

before.content_html:
DNA Structure and the Genome

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the molecule that carries genetic information. Each molecule consists of two strands wound around each other to form a double helix. Each strand is made of repeating units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G).

The two strands are held together by complementary base pairing: A pairs only with T (A–T), and C pairs only with G (C–G). This complementarity is central to how DNA replicates and how genetic information is read. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein. The complete set of genetic information in an organism is called its genome. The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, sequenced the entire human genome and identified the location of around 20,000 protein-coding genes.

Key Fact

DNA base pairing: A pairs with T; C pairs with G. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for one protein. The genome is the complete set of an organism’s DNA. The Human Genome Project mapped all human genes.

Protein Synthesis: Transcription and Translation (Triple Only)

The information stored in a gene is used to build a specific protein through a two-stage process: transcription and translation.

Transcription (in the nucleus): An enzyme called RNA polymerase binds to the gene and reads the template strand of DNA. It builds a complementary strand of messenger RNA (mRNA) using RNA bases (U replaces T in RNA; uracil pairs with adenine). The mRNA strand leaves the nucleus through pores in the nuclear envelope.

Translation (at the ribosome): The mRNA strand attaches to a ribosome. Each set of three bases on the mRNA (called a codon) codes for one specific amino acid. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome; each tRNA has an anticodon complementary to the mRNA codon. Amino acids are joined together in the correct sequence to build a polypeptide chain, which folds into the final protein.

A mutation in the DNA sequence can change the base sequence of the mRNA, which may alter the amino acid sequence of the protein. If the protein’s shape changes, it may no longer function correctly.

Mendel’s Work and the Principles of Inheritance

Gregor Mendel (1822–1884) was a monk working in Brno who carried out carefully controlled breeding experiments with pea plants between 1856 and 1863. He crossed plants with different traits (e.g. tall vs short, round vs wrinkled peas) and recorded the ratios of traits in offspring across thousands of plants. His results led him to propose two key principles: that hereditary ‘factors’ (what we now call alleles) come in pairs, and that one factor can mask the other.

Mendel’s work was largely ignored during his lifetime, partly because he lacked a mechanism to explain his results. When chromosomes and cell division were discovered after his death, scientists realised that Mendel’s hereditary factors were genes on chromosomes. His work was then recognised as the foundation of genetics.

The key terminology you need:

  • Allele — a different version of a gene. We inherit two alleles of each gene, one from each parent.
  • Dominant — expressed whenever present (one or two copies). Capital letter.
  • Recessive — only expressed when two copies are present. Lower-case letter.
  • Homozygous — both alleles the same (BB or bb).
  • Heterozygous — two different alleles (Bb).
  • Genotype — the allele combination (e.g. Bb). Phenotype — the expressed characteristic (e.g. brown eyes).

Punnett Squares and Genetic Crosses

A Punnett square is a grid that shows all possible allele combinations in offspring from a genetic cross. Parent alleles go along the top and down the side; each cell shows the genotype of a possible offspring.

Both parents are carriers of cystic fibrosis (genotype Ff, where f is recessive). What are the possible genotypes and phenotypes of their offspring?

Punnett square: cross Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Genotype ratio: 1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff. Phenotype ratio: 3 unaffected (FF or Ff) : 1 affected (ff). Probability of an affected child = \(\frac{1}{4}\) or 25%. Each pregnancy carries the same probability.

Sex determination: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes; the 23rd pair determines sex. Females are XX; males are XY. A Punnett cross shows a 50% chance of XX (female) and 50% chance of XY (male) in any pregnancy.

Codominance and ABO Blood Groups (Triple Only)

Codominance occurs when both alleles are equally expressed in the heterozygote, so the phenotype is a blend or shows both traits simultaneously. The ABO blood group system illustrates codominance.

Blood group is controlled by one gene with three alleles: IA, IB and IO. IA and IB are codominant with each other; IO is recessive to both.

  • Blood group A: IAIA or IAIO
  • Blood group B: IBIB or IBIO
  • Blood group AB: IAIB (both A and B antigens expressed — codominance)
  • Blood group O: IOIO
Key Fact

ABO blood groups use codominance: IA and IB alleles are both expressed when present together, giving blood group AB (genotype IAIB). Blood group O requires two copies of the recessive IO allele.

lessons.title: Natural Selection, Evolution and Genetic Engineering

before.content_html:
Natural Selection

Evolution is the gradual change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations. The mechanism that drives evolution is natural selection, independently proposed by Charles Darwin (1809–1882) and Alfred Wallace (1823–1913) in the mid-nineteenth century.

The four-step process of natural selection:

  1. Within a population there is variation in heritable characteristics, arising from random mutations and sexual reproduction.
  2. Individuals with characteristics better suited to the environment are more likely to survive long enough to reproduce (‘survival of the fittest’).
  3. These successful individuals reproduce and pass on their advantageous alleles to offspring.
  4. Over many generations the frequency of the advantageous allele increases in the population, gradually changing its characteristics.
Key Fact

Natural selection: variation exists → individuals with advantageous traits survive and reproduce → advantageous alleles passed to offspring → frequency of the advantageous allele increases over generations. This process never acts on an individual during its lifetime — only populations evolve.

A critical misconception to avoid: evolution does not happen in an individual’s lifetime. Giraffes did not ‘grow’ longer necks to reach leaves. Rather, variation in neck length already existed in the population; individuals with longer necks survived and reproduced more successfully, passing on the alleles for longer necks. Over many generations, the average neck length increased.

Evidence for Evolution

Your exam requires knowledge of three named human fossil finds and the use of stone tools as evidence for human evolution:

Ardi (Ardipithecus ramidus) — approximately 4.4 million years old. Discovered in Ethiopia by Tim White’s team (fossils recovered 1992–1994, formally announced 2009). One of the earliest known hominid fossils, showing features of upright walking alongside features suited to tree living.

Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) — approximately 3.2 million years old. Discovered in 1974 by Donald Johanson in Ethiopia. Lucy’s skeletal remains show clear evidence of bipedalism (walking upright on two legs), yet a small braincase closer in size to that of a chimpanzee.

Richard Leakey — palaeoanthropologist who led fossil discoveries in East Africa attributed to hominin species living approximately 1.6 million years ago, including specimens of Homo erectus. These fossils show a larger brain and more sophisticated stone tools than earlier hominids.

Stone tools provide indirect evidence for human cognitive evolution. Increasingly complex tool-making (from basic Oldowan flakes to more refined Acheulean hand axes) correlates with increasing brain size over time.

The pentadactyl limb is the five-digit limb structure shared by all vertebrates, though modified for different functions — the human hand, bat wing, dolphin flipper and horse leg all contain the same set of homologous bones. This is strong evidence for common ancestry.

Antibiotic resistance is natural selection observed in action on a short timescale. When a bacterium acquires a random mutation that allows it to survive exposure to an antibiotic, it survives while others die. It reproduces rapidly, passing on the resistance gene. Over many generations, the resistant strain dominates. This is why completing a course of antibiotics and not overusing them is essential to slow resistance.

Classification: Three Domains

Living organisms are classified using a hierarchical system. This exam uses the three-domain classification proposed by Carl Woese, which divides life into: Archaea (ancient prokaryotes), Bacteria (true bacteria) and Eukarya (all eukaryotes including plants, animals, fungi and protists). Within each domain, organisms are further classified into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. The species is the most precise level: members of the same species can breed and produce fertile offspring.

Selective Breeding

Selective breeding (artificial selection) is the human-directed version of natural selection. Humans select organisms with desirable traits and breed them together. Repeating this over generations concentrates the desired characteristics.

Examples: selectively breeding cows for higher milk yield, wheat for disease resistance, dogs for specific sizes or temperament. A key disadvantage is that it reduces genetic variation within a population (inbreeding), making the population more vulnerable to disease or environmental change. Tissue culture allows selective breeding to be extended to plants: identical plants can be produced from meristem cells and selected for desirable traits.

Genetic Engineering and GM Crops (Triple Only)

Genetic engineering involves inserting a gene from one organism into the DNA of another. The general process:

Step 1 — Identify and isolate the gene: The desired gene (e.g. the human insulin gene) is identified. Restriction enzymes cut the gene from the donor organism’s DNA at specific base sequences, leaving ‘sticky ends’.

Step 2 — Insert into a vector: A vector (commonly a bacterial plasmid) is cut with the same restriction enzyme, leaving complementary sticky ends. The gene is inserted; ligase enzyme joins the sticky ends, sealing the gene into the plasmid.

Step 3 — Transform the host: The recombinant plasmid is introduced into a host cell (e.g. a bacterium such as E. coli). The bacterium then replicates, with each daughter cell containing the new gene and expressing the desired protein.

GM crop example — Bt crops: The bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis naturally produces a protein (Bt toxin) that kills insect pests. The gene for Bt toxin has been inserted into crop plants (e.g. cotton, maize), making the crops resistant to pest damage without needing as many insecticide sprays.

Key Fact

Genetic engineering uses restriction enzymes (cut DNA), ligase (joins sticky ends) and vectors such as plasmids (carry the gene into the host cell). Example: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) gene inserted into crops gives pest resistance without insecticides.

lessons.title: Disease, Pathogens and the Immune Response

before.content_html:
Communicable and Non-Communicable Diseases

Communicable diseases are illnesses spread between organisms by pathogens. Non-communicable diseases are not caused by pathogens and cannot be spread. The two categories can interact: a weakened immune system (from a non-communicable condition) makes a person more vulnerable to infections, while chronic infection can trigger inflammatory damage that leads to non-communicable conditions.

Key Fact

There are four main types of pathogen: bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protists. Bacteria cause disease by producing toxins; viruses invade host cells to replicate; fungi and protists use other mechanisms. Each type requires a different treatment approach.

Named Pathogens You Need to Know

Your specification requires you to know a range of named diseases caused by specific pathogens. The table below groups them by pathogen type.

Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, spread through contaminated water. It produces toxins that cause severe diarrhoea and rapid dehydration. Treatment is rehydration; clean water supplies prevent spread.

Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread through airborne droplets. It primarily infects the lungs, causing persistent cough, weight loss and fever. TB is treated with a long course of antibiotics and remains a leading infectious disease globally.

Helicobacter pylori is a bacterium that colonises the stomach lining. It is a major cause of stomach ulcers and is treated with antibiotics combined with acid-reducing medicines.

Chlamydia is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection. It often has no symptoms but can cause reproductive damage if untreated. It is treated with antibiotics and prevented through safe-sex practices.

HIV attacks the immune system’s helper T-cells, destroying the body’s ability to fight infection. Advanced HIV infection, when the immune system is severely compromised, is called AIDS. HIV is spread through unprotected sexual contact, sharing needles, or mother to child. Antiretroviral drugs prevent progression but cannot cure the virus.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever spread through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals. It causes fever, bleeding and multi-organ failure. Outbreaks are controlled by quarantine, contact tracing and barrier nursing.

Viruses replicate by two cycles. In the lytic cycle, the virus immediately takes over the host cell, replicates rapidly, and bursts the cell to release new viral particles. In the lysogenic cycle, viral DNA integrates into the host cell’s genome and is replicated passively each time the cell divides — it can remain dormant for years before switching to lytic replication.

Chalara ash dieback is caused by the fungus Hymenoscyphus fraxineus. It spreads via windborne spores and has devastated ash tree populations across Europe. There is no effective treatment; management involves removing infected trees to slow spread.

Malaria is caused by the protist Plasmodium, spread by the female Anopheles mosquito acting as a vector. The protist infects and destroys red blood cells, causing fever, chills and anaemia. Prevention focuses on mosquito control (insecticides, bed nets, draining stagnant water); antimalarial drugs reduce severity.

Plant Defences and Plant Pathogens

Plants also suffer from communicable diseases. Pathogens can spread through wind, water, soil and vectors such as insects. Plants defend themselves through physical barriers (the waxy cuticle, cell walls) and chemical defences (antibacterial compounds, toxic secondary metabolites). They also respond to infection with localised cell death to limit the spread of pathogens — a process called the hypersensitive response.

Key Fact

Human non-specific defences include: (1) physical barriers — skin and the mucus-cilia escalator in the airways; (2) chemical barriers — lysozyme in tears and saliva; (3) the inflammatory response — damaged tissues release signals that attract white blood cells to the site of infection.

The Immune Response

If pathogens breach the non-specific barriers, the specific immune system responds. Pathogens carry molecules on their surfaces called antigens. These antigens are recognised as foreign, triggering white blood cells called lymphocytes to produce antibodies. Each antibody is complementary in shape to one specific antigen.

Antibodies work by: clumping pathogens together so phagocytes can engulf them more easily; neutralising bacterial toxins; and marking pathogens for destruction by other immune cells. This specificity — one antibody shape for one antigen — is the key to the adaptive immune response.

After defeating a pathogen, some lymphocytes persist as memory lymphocytes. These can remain for decades. If the same pathogen enters the body again, memory lymphocytes divide and differentiate rapidly, producing large quantities of the correct antibody far faster than the primary response. This rapid secondary response usually prevents symptoms from developing — the person is immune.

Vaccination and Herd Immunity

A vaccination introduces antigens into the body without causing the full disease. The immune system responds by producing antibodies and memory lymphocytes. If the vaccinated person later encounters the real pathogen, their memory cells respond so rapidly that infection is prevented.

When enough people in a community are vaccinated, the pathogen cannot spread easily — each infected person is likely to encounter immune individuals who block onward transmission. This is called herd immunity. It protects vulnerable people who cannot receive vaccines, including those with certain medical conditions.

Antibiotics and Aseptic Technique

Antibiotics kill bacteria or prevent their reproduction. They have no effect on viral infections because viruses replicate inside the host’s own cells — an antibiotic that damaged viral replication would damage the host cell too. Antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection: bacteria with random mutations that confer resistance survive, reproduce and pass on resistance genes, especially when courses are not completed or antibiotics are used inappropriately.

Aseptic technique is essential when culturing microorganisms. Key steps include: sterilising equipment before use (using an autoclave to kill all microorganisms at high pressure and temperature); working near a Bunsen flame to create an upward air current that carries contaminants away; flaming the necks of culture vessels before and after opening; and using sterile pipettes and loops. Agar plates must be incubated at no more than 25°C in school settings to prevent growth of dangerous human pathogens.

In the core practical for investigating the effectiveness of antibiotics, antibiotic-soaked discs are placed on bacterial culture plates. The zone of inhibition — the clear area around the disc where bacteria cannot grow — measures the antibiotic’s effectiveness. A larger zone indicates greater effectiveness against that strain.

lessons.title: Medicines, Monoclonal Antibodies and Lifestyle Disease

before.content_html:
Discovering and Developing New Drugs

New medicines rarely appear quickly. The journey from a promising compound to a licensed drug typically spans more than a decade. Many potential drugs are discovered by screening natural sources — historically, the painkiller aspirin originated from willow bark compounds, and the heart drug digitalis from foxglove plants. Today, pharmaceutical companies also synthesise new molecules in the laboratory and test them computationally before any biological testing begins.

Key Fact

Drug testing has three stages: (1) preclinical testing on cells, tissues and animals; (2) clinical trials on healthy volunteers then patients, using double-blind placebo-controlled design; (3) peer review and regulatory approval. Each stage must be passed before the next begins.

Stage 1 — Preclinical testing: The drug is tested on cell cultures and isolated tissues to assess toxicity and efficacy. If results are promising, it moves to animal testing, which examines dose, toxicity and pharmacokinetics (how the body processes the drug). Preclinical testing cannot predict all human responses, but it filters out the most dangerous compounds.

Stage 2 — Clinical trials: Phase I involves a small number of healthy volunteers to assess safety and find a safe dose range. Phase II involves patients with the target condition, testing for effectiveness and monitoring side effects at a larger scale. Phase III is a large-scale randomised controlled trial. Double-blind design is used: neither the patient nor the clinician knows who receives the active drug and who receives a placebo. This eliminates placebo effect and observer bias. Results are analysed statistically after the trial is unblinded.

Stage 3 — Peer review and approval: Trial results are submitted to regulatory bodies (such as the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency in the UK) and published in peer-reviewed journals. Independent scientists scrutinise the methodology and data before the drug is approved for prescribing.

Monoclonal Antibodies

Monoclonal antibodies are produced by fusing a lymphocyte (which makes a specific antibody but cannot divide indefinitely) with a myeloma cell (a tumour cell that divides without limit but does not make antibodies). The resulting hybridoma cell can both divide without limit and produce a single, specific antibody. Large quantities of identical antibodies are cultured and purified.

Key Fact

Monoclonal antibodies are used in: (1) pregnancy testing — detecting the hormone HCG in urine; (2) cancer diagnosis — binding to tumour antigens to reveal their location; (3) cancer therapy — delivering drugs or radioactive labels directly to tumour cells while sparing healthy tissue.

Pregnancy testing: Early pregnancy is signalled by the hormone human chorionic gonadotrophin (HCG). A home pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies specific to HCG. If HCG is present in the urine sample, the antibodies bind to it; this complex moves along the test strip and triggers a coloured indicator, giving a positive result. If no HCG is present, no complex forms and the result is negative.

Cancer treatment: Some cancer cells display specific antigens not found on healthy cells. Monoclonal antibodies engineered to bind those antigens can be attached to a chemotherapy drug or a radioactive label. When injected, the antibody ‘seeks out’ cancer cells and delivers the toxic payload directly, reducing the collateral damage to healthy tissue that traditional chemotherapy causes. This is sometimes called targeted or ‘magic bullet’ therapy.

Limitations: Producing monoclonal antibodies is expensive and technically complex. They can cause unwanted immune reactions in some patients, and finding a tumour antigen unique enough to target without affecting healthy cells is difficult. Their development has raised ethical questions, particularly around the use of mice to generate the initial lymphocytes.

Non-Communicable Diseases: BMI and Obesity

Body mass index (BMI) is a widely used measure to classify whether a person’s mass is in a healthy range for their height. It is calculated as:

$$\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{mass (kg)}}{\text{height (m)}^2}$$

For adults, a BMI of 18.5–24.9 is generally considered healthy; 25–29.9 is classed as overweight; 30 or above is classed as obese. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnostic measure. It does not distinguish between fat mass and muscle mass, so it can misclassify very muscular individuals. Waist-to-hip ratio is an alternative measure that better reflects abdominal fat distribution and associated health risk.

The relationship between obesity and disease is a correlation, not a simple linear cause. Obesity raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, some cancers and joint problems. However, not all obese individuals develop these conditions and some non-obese individuals do. Other variables — genetics, diet quality, activity level, socioeconomic status — interact with mass to determine health outcomes. Examiners expect students to distinguish between correlation and causation in data questions.

Cardiovascular Disease

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is one of the leading non-communicable causes of mortality. It is strongly associated with lifestyle risk factors: a diet high in saturated fat and salt, physical inactivity, smoking, obesity, high blood pressure and high blood cholesterol. Fatty deposits build up in the walls of the coronary arteries over time — this is called atherosclerosis — narrowing the lumen and restricting blood flow to the heart muscle.

Statins are drugs that reduce blood cholesterol by blocking the enzyme responsible for its synthesis in the liver. Lower cholesterol slows the build-up of fatty plaques in the arteries. Statins are taken daily, reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, but can cause side effects including muscle pain in some patients.

Stents are small metal mesh tubes inserted into a narrowed coronary artery during keyhole surgery to prop it open and restore blood flow. Stents provide immediate relief but do not prevent further plaque build-up in other vessels. Patients may need to take blood-thinning drugs after stent insertion.

More invasive options include coronary artery bypass surgery, where a healthy blood vessel from another part of the body is grafted to bypass the blocked section. In severe cases, an artificial or donor heart may be considered. All surgical interventions carry risk; lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, stopping smoking) remain the most effective primary prevention.

Key Fact

Statins lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting the enzyme that synthesises it in the liver — reducing the rate of plaque formation in arteries. Stents mechanically prop open narrowed arteries. Both reduce cardiovascular risk but neither reverses existing damage; lifestyle change prevents further progression.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the BMI of a person with a mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.80 m. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
practice_questions.marks:
BMI = 72 ÷ (1.80)² = 72 ÷ 3.24 = 22 (kg/m²) [2 significant figures]
• 1 mark for correct substitution: 72 ÷ (1.80)² or equivalent
• 1 mark for correct answer: 22 (kg/m²) with units
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what a double-blind placebo trial is and why this design is used when testing new drugs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Neither patient nor clinician knows who receives the drug or placebo; eliminates both placebo effect (patients' belief in treatment affecting outcomes) and observer bias (clinician's expectations affecting assessment); comparison group (placebo) allows true effect of drug to be measured statistically; result is more reliable.
Secure: Double-blind defined correctly; at least two reasons for the design.
Developing: Double-blind partially defined; one reason given.
Emerging: Placebo mentioned but no explanation of why bias matters.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced in the laboratory.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for:
• A mouse is immunised with the target antigen so its lymphocytes produce specific antibodies.
• Lymphocytes are fused with myeloma (tumour) cells to produce hybridoma cells.
• Hybridoma cells are cultured; they divide without limit and secrete large quantities of the specific antibody, which is then purified.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A patient with blocked coronary arteries is offered a choice between statin medication and a stent procedure.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each treatment option.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Statins — advantages: non-invasive, daily tablet, lower cholesterol reducing further plaque formation; disadvantages: take time to work, potential muscle side effects, do not clear existing blockage. Stents — advantages: immediate restoration of blood flow, effective for severe narrowing; disadvantages: surgical risk, anaesthetic, does not prevent further build-up elsewhere, anti-clotting medication needed post-op. Sustained evaluative comparison: student weighs which is preferable given severity of blockage and patient factors; reaches justified conclusion that severe blockage requires stent + long-term statins and lifestyle change.
Secure: Clear benefits and limitations of both; some comparative weighing; conclusion present.
Developing: Benefits and limitations for each listed; little weighing or comparison; conclusion weak.
Emerging: One or two factual points per treatment; no evaluation.
[9 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text: A pharmaceutical company discovers a new compound that kills the bacteria that cause tuberculosis. Outline the process the company must follow before the drug can be prescribed to patients.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Preclinical testing on cell cultures and tissues (toxicity, efficacy); if safe, animal testing for dose and side effects; Phase I clinical trial on healthy volunteers (safety, dose range); Phase II on patients with TB (effectiveness, monitor side effects); Phase III large-scale double-blind placebo-controlled trial; statistical analysis; submission to regulatory body; peer review of published results; approval before prescribing.
Secure: At least four stages with preclinical → clinical trial → approval sequence correct.
Developing: Preclinical and clinical testing mentioned; stages not clearly ordered; regulatory approval not mentioned.
Emerging: Vague reference to testing; no sequence.
[6 marks — level of response]

practice_questions.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using monoclonal antibodies in cancer treatment compared with conventional chemotherapy.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for:
• Advantage: monoclonal antibodies target only cancer cells displaying the specific antigen, reducing damage to healthy tissue compared with conventional chemotherapy.
• Disadvantage: any one of — expensive to produce; can cause immune reactions in some patients; difficult to find a truly unique tumour antigen; not all cancers have a suitable targetable antigen.
[2 marks]
